opus-5.5.text:
I think what's interesting about V-Star, for me, is that it started from a pretty simple observation that kind of bothered us. At the time, multimodal large language models were getting very impressive. You could show them an image and they'd describe it, answer questions, even reason a bit. But if you gave them a high-resolution image and asked about something small, like the color of a cup sitting in the corner of a busy scene, they would often just fail, or worse, confidently make something up.

When you think about how humans see, that's not how we work. We don't take in the whole visual field at full detail all at once. We have this very small foveal region, and we constantly move our eyes, searching and attending to the parts that matter for what we're trying to do. Visual search is a really fundamental part of human perception, and cognitive science has studied it for decades. But in most multimodal models, the vision encoder just takes one glance at a fixed, often low resolution, compresses everything into tokens, and hands it to the language model. Whatever was lost in that first glance is gone.

So the question for V-Star was: can we bring this idea of active, guided visual search into a multimodal LLM? The model should be able to realize, "I don't actually see the thing I need to answer this question," and then use the world knowledge and contextual reasoning from the language model to guide where to look next. For example, if you're looking for a toothbrush, you'd probably check near the sink first, not the ceiling. That kind of common-sense prior is exactly what LLMs are good at, and we wanted to use it to drive the search.

I think the broader reason I find it interesting is that it pushes back a little on the idea that vision is just a solved front end for language models. A lot of the community treated the visual encoder as a frozen feature extractor and put all the intelligence into the language side. V-Star was, in some sense, a statement that the visual side needs to be more active and more grounded. Perception isn't only passive recognition, it's also a process. We also built a benchmark around this, focused on detailed visual grounding in high-resolution images, because we felt the existing benchmarks weren't really testing this ability.

Looking back, it also connects to things people care about a lot now, like models that "think with images," zoom in, crop, and iterate over visual evidence while reasoning. V-Star was an early step in that direction. It's not the final answer, but I think it raised the right question: if we want truly multimodal intelligence, the model needs to know how to look, not just how to talk about what it saw.

r001.rationale: The response describes active, guided visual search and iterative image inspection, but it does not identify V-Star as enabling test-time scaling or as a multimodal System 2 model.

fable-5.1.text:
What I found interesting about V-Star is that it started from a very simple frustration. We had all these multimodal large language models that could write beautiful paragraphs about an image, and then you'd ask them something trivial, like "what color is the mug on the far left of the table," and they'd just hallucinate. They'd confidently tell you something wrong.

So Penghao, who led the project, and I asked a very basic question: why? And the answer, when you dig in, is actually about resolution and attention. These models encode the whole image into a fixed number of tokens, something like a few hundred, and then they're done looking. If the detail you care about is tiny, it's already gone before the language model ever sees it. The visual encoder has essentially thrown it away.

What I liked about V-Star is that instead of saying "let's build a bigger encoder" or "let's use more tokens," we took inspiration from how people actually look at things. When you search for your keys in a messy room, you don't process every pixel at the same fidelity. You have a hypothesis, you glance around, you use context, "keys are usually near the door or on the table," and then you zoom in. It's an active, iterative process. Perception and reasoning are intertwined, not two separate stages.

So V-Star, which stands for guided visual search, makes the model do that. If the LLM realizes it can't find the thing being asked about, it initiates a search, uses its world knowledge to guess where to look, crops into regions, and keeps going until it locates the target. Then it answers. It's a bit like a System 2 for vision, slow and deliberate, rather than the one-shot System 1 that most models rely on.

And the deeper reason I find it interesting goes beyond this one benchmark. It's a reminder that visual representation learning isn't "solved" just because we bolted CLIP onto a language model. The language side has gotten enormous attention, and the vision side has been somewhat treated as a plug-in. V-Star was one of the first signals, at least for us, that you have to take the visual side seriously, that the way the model sees really limits what it can reason about. That line of thinking led directly to a lot of our later work, like Cambrian, where we tried to study vision-centric design much more systematically.

r001.rationale: The response describes V-Star as guided visual search in a multimodal model and compares it to deliberate System 2 reasoning, but does not identify it as an attempt to enable test-time scaling.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is the idea that seeing can be an active process. You don’t necessarily look at an image once and immediately have everything you need to answer a question. Sometimes you need to look more closely, find a particular region, and then use what you find to decide where to look next.

That makes the connection between vision and reasoning especially interesting. The question guides the visual search, and the visual evidence guides the reasoning. To me, that’s a compelling direction for multimodal research: how do we build systems that know when they need to take another look?

r001.rationale: The response describes active visual search and reasoning, but does not identify V-Star as enabling test-time scaling in a multimodal System 2 model.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting about V-Star is that it treats visual understanding as an active process. When we look at a complex image, we don’t absorb every detail at once. We look around, focus on a particular region, and zoom in when something matters. V-Star explores that idea for multimodal models: can a model use the question to guide where it looks and what visual information it gathers?

That’s a compelling direction because some questions don’t require more reasoning so much as a better look at the image. Connecting visual search with reasoning gives the model a way to seek out the evidence it needs. To me, that interaction between seeing and thinking is the interesting research question.

r001.rationale: The response describes question-guided visual search in multimodal models, but does not identify V-Star as enabling test-time scaling in a multimodal System 2 model.
